Balak thought Balaam did not understand how urgent the situation was nor how great the offered payment.
Balaam’s reply reflected the lesson he had learned in the donkey incident (cp. Numbers 22:20, Numbers 22:35).

Balak attempted to secure Balaam’s curse on Israel, first through a ritual offering and meal that would invoke the gods and Balaam, and second by taking Balaam to see the Israelite camp. • Kiriath-huzoth is an unknown location.

Bamoth-baal (“high places of Baal”) was along the ridge of hills that overlooks the plains of Moab northeast of the Dead Sea (cp. “Bamoth” in Numbers 21:19; Joshua 13:17). It was the first of three locations to which the Moabite king took Balaam so that he could see the sprawling Israelite camp (also Numbers 22:41; Numbers 23:14, Numbers 23:28). From such a high point he could see the Israelites (Numbers 22:11) and perform the ceremonies that Balak hoped would lead to a powerful imprecation (curse) against them.
The number seven was a sacred symbol (also Numbers 23:4, Numbers 23:14, Numbers 23:29; cp. Job 42:8; see “Symbolic Numbers” Theme Note).

As a diviner, Balaam performed rituals to interpret omens and ascertain Israel’s future (cp. Numbers 23:23; Numbers 24:1). Balak had summoned him to pronounce imprecations, but God repeatedly prohibited him from doing so. • It is possible that these sacrifices were connected with the practice of extispicy—the examination of animal livers or other organs for an omen concerning the future. According to ancient Near Eastern texts, this form of fortune-telling was a widely practiced and highly developed art. Such practices were banned from Israel (see Deuteronomy 18:9-14; cp. Ezekiel 21:21).

Instead of cursing Israel, the seer noted their special status (cp. Exodus 19:5-6; Deuteronomy 7:6-9) and observed that God’s blessing had turned a humble people into a great nation (cp. Genesis 12:2-3; Genesis 13:16; Genesis 28:14). Balaam wished for similar good fortune to come his way (Numbers 23:10).

In his first oracle from God (Numbers 23:5, Numbers 23:16), Balaam rehearsed the circumstances that brought him to Moab, emphasized God’s special relation with Israel, and declared his intention of protecting them from harm. • These poetic oracles illustrate the parallelism of Hebrew poetry. Parallel lines reinforce the content by repeating important concepts in a highly structured pattern. • Aram: Aram-naharaim (Genesis 24:10) is another name for North Mesopotamia, where Balaam’s home of Pethor was located (Numbers 22:5). • The eastern hills are a line of mountains in North Syria.

Balak hoped that he would get different results if he changed the venue. The precise location of the plateau of Zophim on Pisgah Peak is unknown, though Pisgah is part of the ridgeline that overlooks the plains of Moab (Deuteronomy 34:1) in the vicinity of Bamoth-baal (Numbers 22:41) and Mount Peor (Numbers 23:28).
This oracle emphasizes God’s faithfulness to his people—he would stay with them and keep all of his promises.
Because of God’s reliable character, Balaam could do nothing but bless Israel.

Since the Lord would follow through on his promises to bless his people (bringing them no misfortune or trouble), Balaam was in no position to reverse God’s intentions. Though God punished the Hebrews for acts of disobedience, his advocacy of Israel’s cause was evident from the time he delivered them from Egypt.

No curse could succeed against Israel because they had been blessed (Numbers 22:12; cp. Genesis 12:2-3; Genesis 22:17-18). Israel was safe from the harm that Moab and Midian sought to inflict through divination (cp. Numbers 24:1); Israel would become famous because God protected them from harm (see Joshua 2:9-11; cp. Numbers 14:13-19).

Disappointed with Balaam’s blessing, Balak hoped that yet another change of location would produce different results. Though the location of Mount Peor is unknown, this place was probably near a worship site of Baal of Peor (cp. Numbers 25:3, Numbers 25:5) and the Beth-peor of Deuteronomy 3:29; Deuteronomy 34:6, where Moses was buried.

Unlike previously (Numbers 23:3, Numbers 23:15), Balaam did not resort to divination this time. He already knew that auguries and omens could not harm Israel (Numbers 23:23), so he quit looking for them. Instead, Balaam was directly inspired by the Spirit of God.
The third oracle contains another description of God’s plan to bless Israel.
God’s love for his people was reflected in the blessings he showered upon them.

The Lord’s favor is emphasized by the comparison of Israel’s situation with groves and gardens that have access to abundant water. Their growing population already reflected God’s blessing (Numbers 24:7), as mentioned in Numbers 23:10. This would also become clear in the second registration (ch Numbers 26:1-65).

God’s blessing would enable the Israelites to overcome their enemies (see Numbers 24:15-24). • Agag was an Amalekite king defeated by Saul (1 Sam 15:7-9, 32-33). The Amalekites, a desert people, were traditional enemies of the Hebrews (cp. Numbers 14:45; Exodus 17:8-16), and it is likely that Agag was the traditional designation for their king. Since God brought Israel out of Egypt, he fought on their behalf, like a warrior and like a wild animal (ox and lion; Numbers 24:8-9). • Blessed . . . cursed: See Genesis 12:3; Genesis 27:29.
Balak clapped his hands in reproach (cp. Job 27:23; Lamentations 2:15).

let me tell you what the Israelites will do to your people in the future: Since Balak sought to curse Israel, he and his people would be cursed (Numbers 24:9). The damage that Balak hoped to inflict on Israel would fall on Moab.

This prophecy provides more specific details than the first three. Based on another vision from the Almighty (Numbers 24:16), it lists some of the enemies that Israel would defeat in the future and predicts the emergence of an outstanding leader who would play a major role in these military victories (Numbers 24:17).

A star was a symbol for a king (cp. Isaiah 14:12; Matthew 2:1-10), and a scepter was an image of power and majesty (cp. Genesis 49:10; Psalm 45:6). King David fits the description historically. The Moabites, whose defeat is mentioned in Numbers 24:17, were among the many peoples conquered during his reign (2 Sam 8:2), though Moab remained a dangerous enemy of Israel after David’s time (cp. 2 Kgs 3:1-27; Isaiah 15:1–16:14; Jeremiah 48:1-47). Many interpreters have extended the image beyond David. Christians identify Jesus of Nazareth with a star (cp. Matthew 2:2; 2 Pet 1:19; Revelation 2:28; Revelation 22:16) and a scepter (cp. Hebrews 1:8). • The people of Sheth were probably the ancient Sutu, though it might refer to Edom/Seir (also conquered by David; Numbers 24:18), Ir (or Ar) of Moab (Numbers 24:19; cp. Numbers 21:28), or Amalek, one of Israel’s earliest and most persistent enemies (Numbers 24:20).

The Kenites, a desert people who occupied some of the same regions as the Amalekites and Midianites, would be destroyed by Assyria. Moses married a Kenite (Judges 1:16; Judges 4:11; cp. Numbers 10:29-32), and the Kenites remained mostly friendly with Israel thereafter (e.g., 1 Sam 15:6; 27:10; 30:27-30).
This verse, like Numbers 22:12, sums up the lesson of the entire incident.

The oracle ends with a word about the rise and fall of invaders from Cyprus (Hebrew Kittim; this term probably referred to a number of Mediterranean people groups; cp. Genesis 10:4; Jeremiah 2:10; Daniel 11:30).

Eber, spelled the same as the ancestor of the Hebrews (cp. Genesis 10:21-25; Genesis 11:10-16), possibly refers to a people beyond the Euphrates River, a region that fits the parallel reference to Assyria (Joshua 24:3; Isaiah 7:20).
Balaam did not yet go back to Pethor (Numbers 31:8).

Acacia Grove: This type of tree thrives in arid regions. From here, Joshua later sent spies across the Jordan, and the Hebrews launched their conquest (Joshua 2:1; Joshua 3:1). • Moabite women: The Moabites and Midianites shared culpability in the episode involving Balaam (Numbers 22:2-4, Numbers 22:7; Numbers 31:8, Numbers 31:15-16).

Israel was camped across the Jordan from Jericho, almost on the eve of conquest, but they plunged to a new low in moral failure and spiritual bankruptcy. Balaam’s advice led to the immorality and apostasy of Baal-peor (Numbers 31:16); he found a way to damage Israel, if not through a curse, then through lust and idolatry. The same temptation to idolatry and immorality existed for the early church (1 Cor 10:6, 11).
The Israelites participated in worship feasts associated with the gods of Moab (see Psalm 106:28).

Baal of Peor might refer to Chemosh (Numbers 21:29) by a different name, but probably Baal (“lord”), the Canaanite god, was included on the list of deities honored by the Moabites. Numerous place-names were formed with this deity’s name (e.g., Baal-gad, Baal-hermon, Baal-meon, Baal-peor), representing shrines for local manifestations of Baal. Peor was a mountain from which Balaam could see the Israelite camp in the plains of Moab; the mountain and the related shrine of Beth-peor (Numbers 23:28; Numbers 25:3, Numbers 25:5, Numbers 25:18; Numbers 31:16; Deuteronomy 3:29; Deuteronomy 4:3, Deuteronomy 4:46; Deuteronomy 34:6; Joshua 13:20; Joshua 22:17) were somewhere in the vicinity of Mount Nebo. • Israel’s idolatry caused the Lord’s anger to blaze against his people; this included a plague (Numbers 25:8-9; Numbers 26:1; cp. Numbers 11:1, Numbers 11:10; Numbers 12:9).

As he had at Sinai (Exodus 32:27-28), the Lord required swift justice. • execute . . . in broad daylight: The guilty parties were perhaps impaled and left out in the sun (see 2 Sam 21:6, 9) so that everyone could see them and learn from their mistakes (cp. 2 Sam 12:12).

Here another Israelite defiled himself with a foreign woman; apparently both Moabite and Midianite women had been involved in the scandal (Numbers 25:1-3, Numbers 25:16-18; Numbers 31:1-2). The man’s sin was particularly brazen, as he apparently disregarded the judgment and mourning around him. • Some suggest that his tent was an unauthorized shrine associated with the worship of Yahweh, and not just Zimri’s dwelling.

Phinehas, acting as a representative of the priestly family, killed Zimri and Cozbi with one thrust of a spear (Numbers 25:7-8), which probably indicates that they were engaged in sexual intercourse. Phinehas’s zeal stopped the plague (Numbers 25:1-3).

Israel’s identity as the Lord’s people was severely threatened by their unfaithfulness on this occasion. Phinehas was as zealous as God in his pursuit of holiness and justice. As a result, Phinehas and his descendants were granted a special status; God made a special covenant of peace with Phinehas, and qualified men in his family inherited a permanent right to the priesthood (cp. Malachi 2:5). This unconditional covenant was similar to that extended to David (see Jeremiah 33:19-22).
The deaths of Zimri and Cozbi helped to purify Israel from its sin; Phinehas’s act had atoning value (see study note on Lev 1:4).
Attack the Midianites and destroy them: This war is recorded in ch Numbers 31:1-54.
As in the first registration, Moses and Eleazar (who had replaced Aaron) instructed the tribal leaders in the tabulation process.

After nearly forty years, Israel again registered their men of military age (cp. chs Numbers 1:1–4:49) as they camped on the plains of Moab . . . across from Jericho. The overall population had changed only slightly, with 603,550 in the first registration and 601,730 in the second. This nearly complete replacement of population (Numbers 26:63-65) showed that the Lord was faithful to Israel in spite of their repeated acts of rebellion.
the sons of Korah did not die that day: See study note on 16:31-33.
The daughters of Zelophehad initiated important legal reform (see Numbers 27:1-11; Numbers 36:1-12).

In spite of warfare, plagues, and punishments, God had been faithful to Israel. The number of male warriors had shrunk by 1,820 compared to the first registration (cp. Numbers 2:32), a difference of 0.3 percent.

The second registration, like the first, was a military one, but it also provided the basis for distributing land to Israel’s tribes in proportion to the tribes’ populations (cp. Joshua 15:1–19:51). • assign the land by lot: Lots were used to seek divine guidance and avoid favoritism in important matters (e.g., Numbers 27:21; 1 Sam 10:20; 14:41-42; Proverbs 18:18; Acts 1:26).
The family of Kohath received special attention as the clan of Aaron, Moses, and Miriam.

The Levites were numbered separately (cp. Numbers 1:47-49; Numbers 3:14-39). • one month old or older: Cp. Numbers 3:15. • they were not given an allotment of land when it was divided among the Israelites: The Levites were given forty-eight towns for their use, but they received no large territory through the process described in Numbers 26:52-56 (Numbers 35:1-8; cp. Numbers 18:23-24).

The registration figures represent an entirely new generation of Hebrews, for everyone who came out of Egypt died in the wilderness except Caleb and Joshua. Joshua inherited Moses’ position as the leader of Israel (Numbers 27:12-23; see “Joshua” Profile), and Caleb later played an important role as well (see “Caleb” Profile). Numbers 26:1-65 documents Israel’s transition from a generation under God’s condemnation (ch Numbers 14:1-45) to a people with a future, as predicted by Balaam’s four prophecies (chs Numbers 23:1–24:25).
Zelophehad’s lack of male heirs created an opportunity to refine the inheritance laws, which would later be refined even further (cp. Numbers 36:1-13).

The entrance of the Tabernacle was the most important public place, where significant decisions were made. The reference to this event in Joshua 17:4 specifically mentions Eleazar, Joshua, and the Hebrew leaders, but omits Moses’ name. These women requested an exception to the law as it stood, and they brought their case to the highest tribal authorities.

Zelophehad had not been part of Korah’s rebellion (Numbers 16:1-50); if he had been, his property rights would apparently have been voided (see Numbers 15:30; cp. 1 Kgs 21:7-16). Israelite society was patriarchal and patrilineal, tracing ancestry and property through the male line. Zelophehad had no sons, but his daughters wanted his family property rights to continue. Zelophehad’s daughters thus made a reasonable appeal for property rights equal to those of males.
Moses took their case before the Lord, who accepted the women’s appeal and established their case as a principle in order to preserve property within families.
The mountains east of the river probably included Mount Nebo (Deuteronomy 32:49), from which Moses viewed the Promised Land just before his death (Deuteronomy 34:1).
Israel would need leadership when they entered the land of Canaan. Joshua was commissioned to succeed Moses.

Israel was on the threshold of a long battle for Canaan; Moses did not want them to flounder without a leader or lose their way like sheep without a shepherd (cp. 1 Kgs 22:17; Ezekiel 34:5; Matthew 9:36).

Joshua had a solid background for the role (cp. Exodus 17:8-16). He had been Moses’ assistant for a long time (Numbers 11:28; cp. Exodus 33:11). He was also one of the faithful spies (Numbers 13:1–14:45) who knew the people of Israel well. Joshua possessed the Spirit and recognized the special presence of God in his life (cp. Numbers 11:25-29). His relationship with God also gave him wisdom for the tasks ahead (e.g., Deuteronomy 34:9). • lay your hands on him: This act symbolized the transfer of authority from an elder statesman to his assistant (cp. Numbers 8:10-14). Moses did this publicly so that Joshua’s leadership would be incontestable.

Joshua assumed only some of Moses’ authority. Moses had face-to-face contact with God (Numbers 12:6-8; Deuteronomy 34:10-12), but Joshua had only indirect access to revelation, since he had to consult with Eleazar the priest on important matters (Numbers 27:21; cp. Exodus 28:30; Leviticus 8:8). Israel would keep military and spiritual leadership separate hereafter.

The Lord accepted special gifts (cp. Numbers 15:3) as a pleasing aroma, a figurative expression describing God’s acceptance and enjoyment of these gifts (see also Genesis 8:21; Leviticus 1:9; Ephesians 5:2; Philippians 4:18). Offerings were made at appointed times according to specific instructions (see Numbers 28:3–29:39).

These two chapters contain information about Israel’s ritual calendar, including a list of required daily, weekly, and monthly offerings and a list of annual religious events. Thus Israel was instructed to worship God “properly and in order” (1 Cor 14:40). The annual cycle of sacrifices involved a tremendous investment of animals, grain, oil, and wine. Israel marked these special days by stopping their normal work, a kind of sacrifice that recognized the importance of these holy days. This annual cycle included eight different occasions for worship, all of which recalled Israel’s relationship with the Lord. Each worship event included a different combination of burnt, grain, liquid, and/or sin offerings. • For details on the grain and liquid offerings, see Numbers 15:1-16. For explanations of the different types of offerings, see Leviticus 1:1–7:38. For a description of Israel’s festivals, see Leviticus 23:1-44. For the New Testament perspective on the Old Testament sacrificial system, see John 1:29; Romans 12:1; Hebrews 9:9-15; Hebrews 10:1-2; 1 Pet 2:5.
they are my food: See study notes on Exod 29:18; Deut 8:2.

The daily offering was the foundation of the sacrificial system. Its practice was instituted at Mount Sinai (see Exodus 29:38-46). • alcoholic drink: Cp. Numbers 6:3; Leviticus 10:9; Deuteronomy 14:26.

Special days called for additional offerings. The Sabbath day required a sacrifice over and above the regular burnt offering and its accompanying liquid offering. Other passages highlight the importance of the Sabbath (e.g., Exodus 20:8-11; Leviticus 23:3; Deuteronomy 5:12-15).
The offering of the first day of each month—the New Moon—called for the sacrifice of bulls, rams, and lambs as burnt offerings, along with a male goat as a sin offering.

The Passover, followed by the Festival of Unleavened Bread, was the first of five great annual festivals; it was held in early spring (March~April). The Passover required no public sacrifices—it was a family occasion celebrated at home (see also Numbers 9:1-4; Exodus 12:1–13:10; Leviticus 23:5-8; Deuteronomy 16:1-8). This festival played a special role in the background of the Last Supper (see Matthew 26:17-19, Matthew 26:26-27; Mark 14:12; John 11:55; John 12:1; John 13:1; John 18:28, John 18:39; John 19:14, John 19:31; cp. 1 Cor 5:7).

The Festival of Harvest was later called the Festival of Pentecost (see Acts 2:1); see also Leviticus 23:15-22. It celebrated the end of the barley harvest and the beginning of the wheat harvest in early summer (May~June). The Greek name Pentecost means “fiftieth day” (i.e., after Passover; see Acts 20:16; 1 Cor 16:8).
the Festival of Trumpets: See also Leviticus 23:23-25.
Ten days later, on the tenth day of the same month: It is celebrated today as Yom Kippur (from Hebrew yom hakkippurim, Leviticus 23:27).
The Day of Atonement was a solemn occasion, a day of fasting (see also Leviticus 16:1-34; Leviticus 23:26-32; Romans 3:23-25; Hebrews 9:7-12, Hebrews 9:23-28).

The Festival of Shelters began on the fifteenth day of the seventh month. It was an eight-day harvest celebration (Numbers 29:12, Numbers 29:35; Exodus 34:22) that required an enormous number of offerings. This harvest festival was an especially joyous occasion and a time for thanksgiving (see Nehemiah 8:13-18). The shelters also reminded the Israelites of dwelling in tents during their wilderness sojourn (see also Leviticus 23:33-43; 1 Kgs 8:1-2).
Public offerings were supplemented by a variety of voluntary individual gifts (cp. Leviticus 23:38).

Vows included promises of offerings (e.g., Hannah’s vow, 1 Sam 1) and pledges of abstinence (e.g., the Nazirite vow, Numbers 6:1-27). Jesus made reference to the instruction regarding vows in the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5:33).

Vows were an important way to express devotion or piety, but were sometimes made in haste and were often forgotten. Voluntary pledges were commonly made on special religious occasions or in times of war. Perhaps the reference to vows and voluntary offerings (Numbers 29:39) prompted the further discussion here (cp. Numbers 15:3; see also Numbers 6:1-21; Leviticus 5:4-5; Leviticus 27:1-34; Deuteronomy 23:21-23). These instructions were applied in the case of Hannah and Elkanah (1 Sam 1:1-28). Such practices, which included fasting, continued into the New Testament period (e.g., Matthew 6:16; Matthew 15:3-9; Acts 18:18; Acts 21:23). Vows of females—young and unmarried or adult and married—were subject to approval by the responsible male who would be a financial partner in the vow. Nobody, male or female, young or old, should make a vow to God and then neglect it.
A young woman was under the authority of her father, who was responsible for her actions and her financial obligations.

When a young Hebrew woman married, she came under the authority of her husband, who could void the obligations of a vow or pledge made by his wife while she was under her father’s authority by nullifying it as soon as he heard about it.
A widow or a divorced woman usually returned to her father’s family (Leviticus 22:13), but a mature single woman who made a vow or pledge was required to fulfill her religious duties.

A married woman also needed the approval of her husband to make vows and pledges. Her husband could nullify her religious promise, but he had to make this decision on the day he heard about it. God did not hold the married woman guilty of breaking this promise if her husband cancelled it in the proper manner (cp. Numbers 30:5, Numbers 30:8, Numbers 30:12). The self-denial mentioned in Numbers 30:13 probably refers to fasting. If he raised no objection, the husband’s silence implied consent. He could not delay in his objection, or he would incur the guilt of a broken vow (cp. Leviticus 5:4-13).

The Lord ordered Moses to lead Israel in a war of retaliation against the Midianites, who had joined the Moabites in leading the Hebrews into idolatry (ch Numbers 25:1-18). The Midianites were a tribal people who inhabited the arid and semiarid regions south and east of Palestine and east of the Jordan River; they were counted among the “people of the east” (Judges 6:3, Judges 6:33; Judges 7:12). They lived in camps or settlements and were famous for their knowledge of desert transportation (cp. Genesis 37:28, Genesis 37:36; Isaiah 60:6). While they were descended from Abraham (Genesis 25:1-2) and had been friendly toward Moses (Exodus 2:15–3:1; cp. Numbers 10:29), the elders of Midian had joined Balak in hiring Balaam to curse Israel (Numbers 22:4, Numbers 22:7), whose presence threatened the peoples of Transjordan (the region east of the Jordan).
Each tribe contributed 1,000 men for the battle, which enabled all of them to gain experience in combat and share in the victory.

Phinehas son of Eleazar (the high priest) led this force of 12,000 into battle. His leadership helped to define this engagement as “holy war,” an act of revenge for the spiritual harm that Midian had inflicted on Israel (cp. Numbers 25:6-18; Numbers 31:15-16). His zeal in this situation (Numbers 25:11, Numbers 25:13) was equal to what he demonstrated in the case of Zimri and Cozbi (Numbers 25:7-8). • Many believe that holy objects of the sanctuary meant the Ark, which the Hebrews sometimes carried into battle (e.g., Numbers 10:35-36; Joshua 6:6; 1 Sam 4:3-11; cp. Numbers 14:44). Others suggest that they were a variety of sacred vessels associated with the Tabernacle rituals (Numbers 3:31; Numbers 4:15; Numbers 18:3; cp. 1 Kgs 8:4; 1 Chr 9:29; 2 Chr 5:5). The Israelites probably took some or all of these holy objects as symbols of God’s participation in their holy war.

The Israelites killed all of the Midianite men in the particular groups they attacked from their camp in the plains of Moab (Numbers 31:12), not all of the people who were part of the larger Midianite confederation (cp. Judges 6:1–8:35). The number of animals and virgins mentioned in Numbers 31:32-35 indicates that the 12,000 Hebrews fought a sizable enemy force.

Balaam son of Beor deserved to die because his counsel “caused the people of Israel to rebel against the Lord at Mount Peor” (Numbers 31:16). Balaam was punished for his villainous deeds (cp. 2 Pet 2:15; Jude 1:11).

After the battle, the Hebrews began the practice that they sometimes followed throughout the period of conquest and beyond (e.g., Joshua 6:1-27; Joshua 8:1-35; Joshua 10:1–11:23). They destroyed their enemies (sometimes the total population), burned towns, and set aside spoils for their own use or as dedicated to the Lord.
towns and villages: These were larger settlements and smaller unfortified encampments.

outside the camp: Probably to keep from contaminating the Tabernacle and all of the people, the returning troops were subjected to purification rituals because of their contact with corpses (Numbers 31:19-24).

Moses was furious: God had commanded total destruction, but the Midianite women who had followed Balaam’s advice and were largely responsible for the apostasy of Baal-peor had wrongly been given clemency.
Only young virgin women were to be spared, since they had not participated in the incident at Baal-peor.
Israelite warriors who had contact with corpses subjected themselves and their equipment to routine, but important, purification rituals (see Numbers 5:1-4; Numbers 19:1-22).

The plunder was divided into two equal parts, with half going to those who fought against the Midianites and half going to the Israelites who stayed behind (cp. 1 Sam 30:21-25). In this sense, everyone participated in the armed conflict, but the relatively small number of warriors each received a larger portion than the much larger number of those who stayed behind.
The total number of animals and young girls who were not killed was quite large, which indicates that Israel fought against many Midianites.
The plunder was distributed according to the principles established in Numbers 31:25-30.

Though it is unusual for no soldiers from an army to be killed in battle, it is not impossible. Classical authors also reported battles in which few or no Roman soldiers were killed. If the Israelites had the advantages of preparation, surprise, and overwhelming force, they could have defeated the Midianites and lost no troops, especially in light of God’s blessing.

The commanders gladly offered gold objects in gratitude for a great victory that resulted in no loss of life (cp. Exodus 30:12). Ancient art and literature indicate that the Midianites and other desert peoples, both males and females, wore gold jewelry as adornment and as a form of portable wealth (e.g., Judges 8:24-26). Moses and Eleazar brought this large collection to the Tabernacle as a memorial of this special event (cp. Numbers 16:39-40; Zechariah 6:14).

vast numbers of livestock: The Israelites had flocks and herds when they left Egypt (cp. Exodus 12:38); they acquired many more animals as loot in the war with Midian (cp. Numbers 31:32-33) and perhaps in their victories over Sihon and Og (Numbers 21:21-35). • Gilead can refer either to the whole northern region of the plateau east of the Jordan (e.g., Numbers 32:29) or only to the part of that territory between the Jabbok and the Arnon.

From the time that Israel occupied the central part of the area east of the Jordan—during the military encounters described in ch Numbers 21:1-35—Israel had been preparing to invade Canaan. At a moment when the Hebrews needed to safeguard their unity, two tribes asked to settle east of the Jordan River.

Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh settled in the land that Israel had recently captured from Sihon the Amorite and Og of Bashan (cp. Numbers 21:21-35). • Ataroth, Dibon, Jazer, Nimrah, Heshbon, and Elealeh have been linked with archaeological sites. • The location of Sibmah is unknown. • Though the location of a town called Nebo is unknown, it was certainly near a mountain or ridge of that same name, which was located along the escarpment that rises above the northern end of the Dead Sea. • The site named Beon is almost certainly the place called “Baal-meon” in Numbers 32:38, which probably corresponds to the ruins at Ma’in.
Moses assumed that Reuben and Gad wanted to stay east of the Jordan River to avoid the dangers that awaited the other tribes in Canaan (cp. chs Numbers 13:1–14:45).

Caleb is identified as a Kenizzite, a descendant of Esau (cp. Genesis 36:10-11). Apparently Caleb was not a native Israelite, but a convert who was so thoroughly integrated into the life and faith of Israel that he was called upon to represent the tribe of Judah when the twelve scouts were sent out to survey the Promised Land (Numbers 13:6).

The Reubenites and Gadites assured Moses that they would not discourage their fellow Israelites and would support the war to its very end. There were still dangers east of the Jordan River, so they wanted to safeguard their livestock and families.

Moses accepted the terms offered by Reuben and Gad. If they joined their kindred in fighting the Canaanites, they would fulfill their end of the agreement and could then return to their settlements east of the Jordan (Numbers 32:22). If they failed to keep their promise, it would be a serious sin against God (Numbers 32:23).
Reuben and Gad did in fact fulfill the agreement (Joshua 4:12-13; Joshua 22:1-9).
Israel’s leaders—Eleazar, Joshua, and the heads of clans—would help enforce Moses’ terms (cp. Joshua 22:1-2) since his death was imminent.
Gad and Reuben reaffirmed their pledge before all of Israel’s leaders.

The tribes of Gad and Reuben, along with half the tribe of Manasseh, settled east of the Jordan (e.g., Deuteronomy 3:12-13; Deuteronomy 4:43; Deuteronomy 29:7-8). These tribes occupied territory and towns taken from King Sihon the Amorite and King Og of Bashan (Numbers 32:33; see Numbers 21:21-35). • Half the tribe of Manasseh suddenly appears in the discussion of territorial distribution. Part of Manasseh settled east of the Jordan River, while another part of the tribe settled in Canaan, west of the Jordan (cp. Joshua 17:1-12; Joshua 22:7).
The precise locations of Atroth-shophan, Jogbehah, and Beth-haran are unknown. Aroer was located on the northern rim of the Arnon canyon.

If names of some of the towns were changed to avoid pagan associations (e.g., “Baal,” the well-known Canaanite god, or “Nebo,” a Babylonian deity; see Isaiah 46:1), the alternate designations are not provided here.

Three clans of Manasseh conquered part of Gilead and Bashan (cp. Deuteronomy 3:13-15; Joshua 13:29-31). The location of Nobah remains uncertain (cp. Judges 8:11). • Towns of Jair: Hebrew Havvoth-jair (cp. Deuteronomy 3:14; Joshua 13:30; Judges 10:4; 1 Kgs 4:13; 1 Chr 2:21-23).
The itinerary contains features that reflect detailed record keeping. This is the only place where Numbers says that Moses kept a record of Israel’s history (cp. Exodus 24:4).

This review of the entire wilderness period contains the longest integrated list of place-names in the Old Testament, from Israel’s departure from Egypt (Numbers 33:3; cp. Exodus 12:37) until their arrival in the plains of Moab, opposite Jericho (Numbers 33:49; cp. Numbers 22:1). The forty-two way stations on this itinerary represent far more than a geographical journey; they recall Israel’s forty-year spiritual pilgrimage. In their travels between Rameses in Egypt (Numbers 33:3) and AcaciaAbel-shittim on the plains of Moab (Numbers 33:49), Israel finally became the people who could invade the land of Canaan and claim the promises God made to Abraham. • This itinerary does not provide enough data to plot an accurate, specific route. Most of the places cannot be identified with certainty; many of the sites appear nowhere else in the Hebrew Bible, and there are not enough clues to pinpoint their locations precisely. Furthermore, this list is partial or selective, omitting some of the place-names mentioned earlier in the journey.
left defiantly: See Exodus 14:8.
defeated the gods of Egypt: See Exodus 6:6; Exodus 12:12. This historical review draws attention to those special events that forced Pharaoh to allow the Israelite exodus from Egypt.
For Israel’s wilderness itinerary between Rameses and the desert of Sinai, see Exodus 13:17–19:1.
Etham: See Exodus 13:20.
Elim remains impossible to identify with certainty, but it may have been the oasis (with springs and palm trees) at Wadi Gharandel.
The entry for Rephidim (see study note on 20:13) adds a reminder of Israel’s rebellion there (Exodus 17:1-7).

Tradition associates the wilderness of Sinai with a mountainous region in the southern Sinai Peninsula near Jebel Musa (Arabic for “mountain of Moses”), though scholars have suggested other locations.
Kibroth-hattaavah . . . Hazeroth: See Numbers 11:34–12:16.
The journey between Sinai and Kadesh. Our ability to locate the named sites depends on the identification of Mount Sinai.
Most of the place-names in this section appear nowhere else in the Old Testament.
Moseroth was also called “Moserah” (Deuteronomy 10:6). This is where Aaron died and was buried (cp. Numbers 20:22-29; Numbers 33:37-39).
Ezion-geber (cp. Deuteronomy 2:8) was located near the northern end of the Gulf of Aqaba.
Israel was residing in Kadesh (Numbers 13:26; Numbers 27:14; “Kadesh-barnea,” Numbers 32:8) when the spies reported on their trip through Canaan.
Israel traveled from Kadesh to the plains of Moab.
These details about Aaron’s death (cp. Numbers 20:22-29) and his age show that he was about three years older than Moses (cp. Deuteronomy 31:1-2; Deuteronomy 34:7).
Good candidates for the locations of most of these sites are found east of the Jordan between the southern Arabah and the plains of Moab, opposite Jericho.
Almon-diblathaim is probably the same place as “Beth-diblathaim” (Jeremiah 48:22), also mentioned in the famous Mesha Inscription (see study note on Num 21:26).

After the Israelites reached the plains of Moab opposite Jericho (Numbers 22:1), they camped there for the rest of the period covered in Numbers (see Numbers 36:13) and Deuteronomy (Deuteronomy 34:8). While they were camped there, God gave Israel specific instructions for dealing with the population of Canaan. The Lord commanded his people to destroy the people groups that occupied Canaan and to obliterate all vestiges of their religious practices (cp. Exodus 23:23-33; Exodus 34:11-17; Deuteronomy 7:1-6; Deuteronomy 12:2-4; Joshua 23:4-8). Moses’ commands included the destruction of their carved and molten images (cp. Leviticus 26:1) and the demolition of their pagan shrines (see Deuteronomy 12:2-3).
distribute the land . . . by sacred lot: See Numbers 26:53-56. Numbers 34:1-29 describes the boundaries of the land of Canaan, which they would soon conquer and divide.

Israel failed to carry out God’s instructions (Numbers 33:51-53) and suffered the consequences predicted here (see Judges 1:1–2:5; Judges 2:11–3:6). Israel’s enemies in the period of the judges were like splinters and thorns (Numbers 33:55), harassing them militarily and spiritually (cp. 2 Cor 12:7).

Numbers 34:1-29 gives the borders of the land of Canaan, which Israel was to settle according to the guidelines in Numbers 26:52-56. Ever since the call of Abraham (Genesis 12:1-7), the Promised Land of Canaan had stood at the heart of the Old Testament story. Though an entire generation of Hebrews died in the wilderness because they refused to believe the report of the faithful spies (Numbers 13:1-33), God had reaffirmed his promise of land (Numbers 33:53). Here, God reviewed the plan and identified the boundaries of the Promised Land in an idealized form (cp. Joshua 13:1–19:51; Ezekiel 47:1–48:35). Old Testament Israel did not possess the exact extent of the territory described here (though it came close in the days of David and Solomon; e.g., 2 Sam 24:1-9), but these borders describe the region of Canaan as generally defined by Egyptian texts dating 1500–1200 BC (the period of the Hebrew invasion). The region actually occupied by Israel changed from time to time.

Portions of the southern boundary of Canaan were familiar to Israel from earlier experiences in the wilderness of Zin on the northwestern edge of Edom (see chs Numbers 13:1–14:45). This southern frontier ran east to west in an arc from the southern end of the Dead Sea to the Mediterranean Sea.

From the southern end of the Dead Sea, the boundary ran through Scorpion Pass toward Zin (cp. Numbers 13:21). The southernmost point was Kadesh-barnea (cp. Numbers 13:26). Hazar-addar and Azmon are unknown.

The Brook of Egypt (not to be confused with the Nile) designates the wadi that separates the land of Canaan from Egypt; it drains toward the Mediterranean Sea (cp. 1 Kgs 8:65). In Old Testament times, Israel exercised little control over this southern coastal region.

The natural western boundary of Canaan was the Mediterranean coast (Numbers 34:6). The northern boundary began at the Mediterranean and ran eastward to Mount Hor somewhere in the Lebanon range (not the place of Aaron’s death, Numbers 20:22-29). • Lebo-hamath: Cp. Numbers 13:21; 1 Kgs 8:65; Amos 6:14.
Sea of Galilee: Its eastern edge (literally shoulder) is the ridge that rises rather abruptly from its eastern shoreline.

The natural eastern border of Canaan followed the Jordan River down to the Dead Sea. As part of the Great Rift Valley, the Jordan and the Dead Sea were formidable, though not impassable, barriers. This boundary excluded the lands east of the Jordan that were occupied by Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh. Those settlements were not part of Canaan per se and stood outside the Promised Land as originally defined.

you are to divide . . . by sacred lot: Cp. Numbers 26:55-56. Because of the settlement of two and a half tribes (Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh) in Transjordan (cp. Numbers 32:33), Canaan was to be divided among the nine and a half remaining tribes.
Eleazar (the high priest) and Joshua (the political leader) were to divide the land among the remaining tribes. The ten tribal leaders who would help them are listed in Numbers 34:19-28.

Caleb son of Jephunneh is the only tribal leader who appears elsewhere in Numbers (Numbers 13:6, Numbers 13:30; Numbers 14:6-38). Nearly all of the older generation had already died during the wilderness period (Numbers 26:63-65), but the two faithful spies were still leading their people.

The tribe of Levi received no territory, so ch Numbers 35:1-34 describes their allotment of 48 towns dispersed among the territories of Israel’s other tribes (see Joshua 21:1-45; see also Leviticus 25:32-34; 1 Chr 13:2; 2 Chr 11:14). Just as the Levites had lived in the center of the Israelite camp during the wilderness period (cp. Numbers 2:17), in the Promised Land they were to live among the other tribes and have a leavening influence among them (see Deuteronomy 33:9-10; 2 Chr 17:7-9; 19:8-11; 35:3). The cities and their surrounding pastureland were not a “homeland” (cp. Numbers 18:23; Numbers 26:62) but only a tiny fraction of the Canaanite territory dispersed among the other tribes.

Readers have long attempted to explain the alleged contradiction between the 1,500 feet and the 3,000 feet. If the Hebrews conceived of a town as a fixed point, then the square of territory around each town would measure 3,000 feet on each side. Another solution is to see a distinction between pastureland (Numbers 35:4) and larger pastureland (Numbers 35:5) around the town. On the basis of this text, some Jewish interpreters restricted the distance that one could walk on the Sabbath to 3,000 feet (2,000 cubits) from home.

Six of the Levites’ towns had a special purpose as cities of refuge, places where a person who has accidentally killed someone can flee for safety. This unusual institution illustrates the humanitarian aspect of Hebrew law (see also Deuteronomy 4:41-43; Deuteronomy 19:1-13; Joshua 20:1-9). These six Levitical towns provided a safe haven in cases of accidental or involuntary manslaughter (cp. Exodus 21:12-14). Just as the forty-eight Levite towns were widely distributed across Israel’s territories, the six cities of refuge were dispersed so they would be widely accessible (see Joshua 20:7-8). These designated settlements supplemented the role of the altar as a temporary place of asylum (e.g., 1 Kgs 1:50-53; 2:28-34; cp. Exodus 21:14). Other ancient peoples provided special places of asylum or refuge, often at the altar (see Exodus 21:12-14; 1 Kgs 2:28-34), but only ancient Israel established whole settlements as places of sanctuary, reflecting a special interest in social justice.
protection from a dead person’s relatives who want to avenge the death: Justice was enacted through vengeance at the hand of a designated avenger, usually a relative.

Israelites, foreigners living among you, and traveling merchants. Anyone: The same law applied impartially to everyone; Israel had one standard of justice, not two (one for citizens, another for noncitizens), as in many societies (see also Leviticus 19:15; Deuteronomy 1:16-17; 1 Tim 5:21; James 2:2-4).

The Old Testament makes a clear distinction between deliberate murder and involuntary manslaughter (Numbers 35:11, Numbers 35:22-23; Exodus 21:12-14; cp. Numbers 15:22-31). Murder required a penalty of execution, but an accidental death did not. The cities of refuge provided protection only for those who killed another person by accident. • The use of a weapon was proof of malicious intent.
The avenger was the victim’s closest relative; he was responsible for putting the murderer to death, carrying out the vengeance that justice required (Genesis 9:6).

Here are some instances in which a victim died but was not murdered through an intentional act of violence. The cities of refuge were created as places of safety for people who were responsible for such accidental deaths.

If the slayer was cleared of the murder charge in his trial or hearing before the community (cp. Deuteronomy 19:11-12), he had to remain in the city of refuge to which he fled, and the avenger was not supposed to seek revenge, because the slayer was not guilty of murder. • until the death of the high priest: The priest’s death probably provided a kind of expiation for the blood that had been shed; even though the slayer was innocent of murder, human bloodshed had polluted the land (Numbers 35:33; cp. Genesis 4:10-11).

The slayer still suffered a penalty for the death he had caused since he was restricted to a city of refuge until he or the high priest died. But after the death of the high priest, the slayer was free to return to his own home, and the avenger was not to seek revenge.
All murderers were condemned to death, but their conviction required a high standard of evidence—the testimony of two or more witnesses (cp. Deuteronomy 17:6; Deuteronomy 19:15).

The payment of a ransom (monetary compensation) to free a convicted murderer from execution was prohibited, since the death penalty was required (cp. 2 Sam 21:2-9). Similarly, the slayer in an involuntary manslaughter could not pay a ransom to get around his confinement in a city of refuge.

for murder pollutes the land: If the slayer in either a homicide or involuntary manslaughter were not dealt with as commanded, God regarded the land as polluted, because human bloodshed required death (Genesis 4:10-11; Genesis 9:6; contrast Exodus 21:29-30; see also Leviticus 18:28; Ezekiel 36:17-18; Hosea 4:2-3). In its stern warning about the evil of murder, this entire passage highlights the absolute value of human life (Exodus 20:13).

The Lord lived among the people of Israel even as the Tabernacle stood in the middle of the Hebrew camp (see chs Numbers 1:1–4:49). This meant that they must not defile their land by ignoring God’s commands or by failing to uphold justice (cp. Numbers 5:1-4).

Women who inherited land might marry men from another tribe; their land would then be lost by their ancestral tribe and transferred to their husband’s tribe. The Year of Jubilee (Leviticus 25:8-55) normally provided the means for land to return to its original owner, but it pertained only to land that was sold, not to land acquired through marriage.
The five daughters of Zelophehad had petitioned for, and had been granted, equitable property rights (Numbers 27:1-11). Here the ramifications of that decision are discussed.
The Lord readily provided the justice that the men of the tribe of Joseph (i.e., of the tribe of Manasseh, the son of Joseph) sought in their petition.
These stipulations resolved the quandary, guaranteeing the stability and continuity of the tribal land allotments.

As they had been instructed, Zelophehad’s five daughters all married cousins on their father’s side, keeping their father’s allotment within his clan. Marriage to a first cousin was acceptable in ancient Hebrew society (cp. Leviticus 18:1-30, Leviticus 20:1-27; see also 1 Chr 23:22) as well as in other Near Eastern cultures.

Commands and regulations might refer to legal pronouncements from the whole book (cp. Leviticus 27:34) or only to those given on the plains of Moab (Numbers 26:1–36:13). • All that remained to make the Israelites ready to enter Canaan was for Moses to remind them of their history and covenant obligations—the subjects of the book of Deuteronomy.
